nodeData.note: How soil works: life in the soil, texture, pH, water, testing and soil carbon.

children.note: Soil is alive: billions of organisms in every handful feed on plant carbon and on each other, recycling nutrients and building structure. Understanding this web is the basis of biological farming.

The physical and chemical basics every farmer should know: how soil forms, its texture and structure, compaction, pH and liming, nutrient holding (CEC), salt problems, the main soils of East Africa and India, and how to stop erosion.

How soil stores and supplies water, and how to use it well: field capacity and wilting point, irrigation and organic fertigation, mulching, water harvesting, drainage, water quality and drought resilience.
How to tell whether a soil is healthy, from simple spade and water tests in the field to laboratory analysis. Includes how to sample correctly and read a soil report.

How soils store carbon, which farm practices build it, how much evidence backs them, and the limits. Also covers soil nitrous oxide and methane, measuring carbon, carbon credits and drought resilience.

nodeData.note: Soil is alive: billions of organisms in every handful feed on plant carbon and on each other, recycling nutrients and building structure. Understanding this web is the basis of biological farming.

children.topic: What the soil food web is
children.note: The soil food web is the community of organisms living in soil and the feeding links between them. Energy enters through plants and dead organic matter and passes from microbes to the animals that eat them.
Green plants capture sunlight and push carbon into the soil as roots, root exudates and dead leaves. Almost all soil life depends on this carbon, directly or indirectly.

manas.q: Where does almost all the energy in the soil food web come from?

children.note: Primary decomposers (bacteria, fungi) feed on organic matter and exudates. Grazers such as protozoa, nematodes and micro-arthropods eat them, and predators eat the grazers.
This web recycles nutrients, builds soil structure, suppresses some diseases and breaks down residues. A biological product works only if it can find food and a home in this web.
Soil holds a huge diversity of life, from microscopic bacteria to earthworms and insects. Each group does a different job in the system.
Tiny single-celled organisms and the most numerous group in soil. They decompose simple compounds, cycle nutrients, and some fix nitrogen or solubilise phosphorus.
A gram of fertile soil usually holds hundreds of millions to around a billion bacterial cells. Most of them have never been grown in a laboratory.

manas.q: Roughly how many bacteria live in one gram of fertile soil?

links.label: 📄 Source: FAO – State of knowledge of soil biodiversity (2020)

children.note: Examples include nitrogen fixers (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum), nitrifiers (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), phosphate solubilisers (Bacillus, Pseudomonas) and decomposers.
Bacteria produce sticky sugars (polysaccharides) that bind fine particles into micro-aggregates. This helps create pore space for air and water.
Fungi grow as long thread-like hyphae that can bridge gaps between soil particles. They break down tough material such as lignin and cellulose in straw and wood.
Saprophytic fungi digest dead plant material, especially woody and fibrous residues that bacteria handle poorly. They are important in making stable organic matter.
Mycorrhizal fungi live in partnership with roots: the plant feeds them sugars and the fungi extend the root system to fetch phosphorus, zinc and water. Most crops form arbuscular mycorrhiza (AMF).

manas.q: What do arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi give the plant in exchange for sugars?

children.note: Some fungi such as Trichoderma attack disease fungi, while others like Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia cause root diseases. A diverse community helps keep pathogens in check.
Fungal networks are easily broken by ploughing and harmed by some fungicides. Soils under frequent tillage tend to become more bacteria-dominated.
Actinomycetes are filament-forming bacteria, such as Streptomyces, that look a little like fungi. They decompose tough materials and work well in drier, neutral to alkaline soils.
The pleasant smell of freshly dug or wet soil comes largely from geosmin, a compound made by Streptomyces. A sweet earthy smell is a good sign of active biology.

manas.q: Which organisms produce geosmin, the 'earthy' smell of healthy soil?

children.note: Many antibiotics used in medicine, such as streptomycin, were first found in soil Streptomyces. In soil these compounds help them compete and can suppress some pathogens.
Protozoa are single-celled animals (flagellates, amoebae and ciliates) that mainly eat bacteria. They are most active in the moist zone around roots.
Bacteria hold more nitrogen than protozoa need, so when protozoa eat bacteria they release the extra nitrogen as ammonium near the root. This is often called the microbial loop.

manas.q: Why does protozoa grazing on bacteria release plant-available nitrogen?

children.note: Healthy soils commonly contain thousands to tens of thousands of protozoa per gram. Their numbers rise quickly when bacteria multiply.

links.label: 📄 Source: FAO – State of knowledge of soil biodiversity (2020)

children.note: Nematodes are tiny unsegmented worms. Most are beneficial, feeding on bacteria, fungi or other nematodes; a minority are plant parasites.
Bacterial-feeders, fungal-feeders, predators and omnivores recycle nutrients and regulate other populations. Plant-parasitic types such as root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne) damage roots.

manas.q: Are most soil nematodes plant pests?

children.note: A balanced nematode community with many predators and omnivores suggests a stable, undisturbed soil. Dominance by plant parasites signals a problem.
Arthropods include mites, springtails, beetles, ants, termites and millipedes. They shred residues, mix soil and eat other organisms.
Millipedes, woodlice and some mites chew leaves and straw into small pieces. This greatly increases the surface area that microbes can attack.
In East African and Indian drylands, termites and ants are major soil engineers. They move soil, build channels and break down tough dry residues.
Earthworms swallow soil and organic matter and leave behind casts rich in available nutrients. Their burrows improve drainage, aeration and root growth.

Litter-dwellers live in surface litter, topsoil-dwellers burrow horizontally, and deep-burrowers make vertical channels. Compost worms like Eisenia fetida are litter-dwellers and do not survive well in field soil.
Casts are richer in available nutrients and microbes than surrounding soil and form stable aggregates. They are a visible sign of a working soil.

manas.q: Why are earthworm casts valuable to plants?

children.note: The rhizosphere is the thin layer of soil, a few millimetres thick, directly influenced by living roots. It is the busiest part of the soil food web.
Roots leak and actively release sugars, amino acids, organic acids, mucilage and signalling compounds. A meaningful share of the carbon a plant fixes ends up in the soil this way.

manas.q: Name three kinds of compounds found in root exudates.

children.note: In return for exudates, rhizosphere microbes release nutrients, make growth hormones and help defend roots. Plants partly shape which microbes gather around them.
Microbial numbers near roots are many times higher than in bulk soil away from roots. This is why biofertilizers are applied to seed or roots, where food is available.
Cover crops, intercrops and perennial plants keep feeding the rhizosphere between main crops. Long bare fallows starve soil life.
Soil organic matter is everything in soil that was once alive, from fresh residues to highly decomposed material. Though often only a few percent of soil weight, it drives fertility.
SOM includes living organisms, fresh residues, partly decomposed material and stable organic matter. It holds nutrients and water and feeds soil life.
Labs usually measure soil organic carbon (SOC). Organic matter is roughly 58% carbon, so SOM is commonly estimated as SOC × 1.72.

manas.q: How is soil organic matter usually estimated from organic carbon?

children.note: The active pool (fresh residues, microbial biomass) turns over in months to a few years and supplies nutrients. The stable pool persists for decades and builds structure and holding capacity.
Organic matter increases water-holding capacity, nutrient-holding (CEC), buffering against pH change and aggregate stability. In sandy and tropical soils it is often the main source of CEC.
Humus is the dark, well-decomposed part of organic matter that resists further breakdown. It gives soil its dark colour and holds nutrients and water.

Scientists now see stable organic matter mainly as microbial residues and plant compounds protected inside aggregates or bound to clay, rather than special giant 'humic' molecules. Protection, not chemistry alone, keeps carbon in soil.
Glomalin is a sticky glycoprotein linked to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. It coats hyphae and helps glue soil particles into stable aggregates.

manas.q: Which group of fungi is associated with glomalin, and what does it do?

children.note: Add compost, manure and crop residues; keep living roots; reduce tillage; and avoid burning. Gains are slow and are usually measured over years, not one season.
Soil organisms turn nutrients locked in residues and minerals into forms plants can take up. They also store nutrients in their own bodies, reducing losses.
Nitrogen moves between air, organic matter, microbes and plants. Most soil nitrogen is held in organic forms that microbes must release.
Some bacteria convert air nitrogen (N2) into ammonia. Rhizobium does this in legume root nodules, while Azotobacter and Azospirillum do it in the root zone or soil.

manas.q: What is biological nitrogen fixation?

children.note: Microbes break down organic nitrogen in residues and manure to ammonium. Grazing by protozoa and nematodes speeds this up.
Bacteria such as Nitrosomonas convert ammonium to nitrite and Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate. Nitrate is easily taken up but also easily leached.

manas.q: Which bacteria carry out the two steps of nitrification?

children.note: In waterlogged, low-oxygen soil, bacteria turn nitrate into nitrous oxide and N2 gas that escape to air. Nitrate can also leach below the roots after heavy rain.
When residues with lots of carbon and little nitrogen (like straw) are added, microbes take up soil nitrogen and crops may turn yellow for a while. A C:N below about 25:1 usually avoids this.
Phosphorus does not cycle through the air and is easily locked up by calcium in alkaline soils or iron and aluminium in acid soils. Biology helps release it.
Phosphate-solubilising bacteria and fungi release organic acids that free phosphate bound to calcium, iron or aluminium.
Microbes and roots release phosphatase enzymes that free phosphate from organic matter.
Mycorrhizal hyphae reach far beyond the root's depletion zone and bring phosphorus back to the plant. This matters most in low-P soils.
Plants take carbon dioxide from the air and pass it to soil through roots and residues. Microbes respire most of it back, while a part is stored as stable organic matter.
Soil respiration (CO2 release) is a measure of how active soil life is. Moderate, steady respiration with ongoing residue inputs is healthy.
Carbon stays longest when it is held inside aggregates or bound to clay particles. Practices that build aggregates help soils store more carbon.
Microbes also help release potassium, sulphur, zinc and iron. Some make siderophores, molecules that grab iron and make it available to roots or keep it from pathogens.
Soil structure is the way sand, silt, clay and organic matter clump together into aggregates with pores between them. Good structure lets water in and roots and air through.
Bacterial glues bind clay into micro-aggregates; fungal hyphae, roots and glomalin bind these into larger macro-aggregates. Earthworms and termites also build aggregates.

manas.q: Name three biological 'glues' or binders that build soil aggregates.

children.note: Large pores drain water and let air in; small pores store water for plants. A crumbly structure with both sizes supports roots and soil life.
Healthy soil breaks into rounded crumbs, has many root channels and worm holes, and holds together in water. Poor soil forms hard clods, crusts or dense layers.
Many common practices damage the soil food web. Knowing the causes helps farmers protect the organisms that biological inputs depend on.
Repeated ploughing breaks fungal networks and aggregates, exposes organic matter to rapid breakdown and leaves soil bare. Organic matter and earthworm numbers usually decline.

manas.q: Give two ways frequent ploughing harms soil life.

children.note: Broad-spectrum fungicides, fumigants and some soil insecticides kill beneficial organisms as well as targets. Heavy use of ammonium-based fertilisers can acidify soil over time.
Burning straw and stubble destroys organic matter and nitrogen, heats the topsoil and kills organisms near the surface. It also pollutes the air, as seen with paddy straw burning in north India.
Uncovered soil is baked by the sun, crusted by rain and washed away. The topsoil lost carries most of the organic matter and life.
Heavy machinery and grazing on wet soil squash pores and starve organisms of air. Waterlogged soils lose nitrogen and favour root-rot organisms.
Growing the same crop repeatedly narrows the food supply for soil life and lets pests and diseases build up. Rotations and mixtures support a more diverse web.
Practices that keep the soil covered, keep living roots, add diverse organic inputs and reduce disturbance help rebuild soil life.
Minimise disturbance, keep the soil covered, keep living roots as long as possible, increase plant diversity and integrate animals or manure. These are the common principles of soil health.
Well-made compost adds organic matter and a wide range of microbes. It is also an ideal carrier to multiply biofertilizers before field application.
Biofertilizers add useful organisms but they complement, rather than fully replace, nutrients from manures or fertilisers. They establish best in soils with organic matter and moisture.
Short videos on this topic from universities, extension services and experienced growers. Opens YouTube.

nodeData.note: The physical and chemical basics every farmer should know: how soil forms, its texture and structure, compaction, pH and liming, nutrient holding (CEC), salt problems, the main soils of East Africa and India, and how to stop erosion.

children.note: Soil is weathered rock mixed with living and dead organic material, built up slowly over long periods. Knowing how it formed explains why soils differ from field to field.
Parent rock, climate, living organisms, slope (relief) and time together decide what kind of soil develops. Change one factor and you get a different soil.

manas.q: What are the five soil-forming factors?

children.note: Heat, cold, water and roots break rock physically, while water, acids and microbes change its minerals chemically. Warm, wet tropics weather rock deeply; dry areas much less.
A dug pit shows layers: an organic layer on top, dark topsoil (A), subsoil where clay and iron collect (B), then weathered parent rock (C). Most roots and life sit in the topsoil.

manas.q: Which soil layer holds most roots and soil life?

children.note: A good loam is roughly half solids (mostly minerals with a small share of organic matter) and half pore space shared between air and water. The pore half matters as much as the solids.
New topsoil forms far more slowly than erosion can remove it, so a few heavy storms on bare land can undo centuries of formation. Protecting topsoil comes first.
Texture is the share of sand, silt and clay particles in the mineral part of soil. It sets how fast water drains, how much is stored and how well nutrients are held.
In the common USDA scale, sand is 2–0.05 mm, silt 0.05–0.002 mm and clay below 0.002 mm. Gravel and stones above 2 mm are not part of texture.

manas.q: What is the size limit for clay particles?

children.note: The texture triangle turns the three percentages into a class name such as sandy loam or clay loam. A loam has a balanced mix and is often the easiest soil to farm.

manas.q: What tool converts sand/silt/clay percentages into a texture class?

children.note: Sandy soils drain fast, warm early and hold few nutrients; clay soils hold water and nutrients but can be sticky, slow-draining and hard when dry. Silty soils crust easily.
Moisten a walnut-sized ball, then squeeze it between thumb and finger into a ribbon. Gritty means sand, silky means silt, sticky with a long ribbon means clay.

manas.q: In the feel test, what does a long sticky ribbon indicate?

children.note: Half-fill a jar with soil, add water and a pinch of salt or soap, shake well and leave it. Sand settles in a minute, silt within hours and clay over a day or more; measure the layers.

manas.q: In the jar test, which particle settles first?

children.note: You cannot practically change texture on a field scale. You manage it instead: organic matter helps sand hold water and helps clay drain and crumble.
Structure is how particles clump into crumbs (aggregates) with pores between them. Unlike texture, structure can be improved or destroyed by how you farm.
Aggregates are small clumps of sand, silt, clay and organic matter. The spaces between and within them let air, water and roots move through soil.

manas.q: Which can a farmer change quickly: texture or structure?

children.note: Granular crumbs are ideal for topsoil; blocky and prismatic shapes are common in subsoil; platy layers block roots and water; massive or single-grain soil has no useful structure.
Roots, fungal threads, sticky microbial products (including glomalin from mycorrhizal fungi) and earthworm casts bind particles into stable crumbs.

manas.q: Name two living sources of the glue that holds soil aggregates together.

children.note: Frequent tillage, bare soil under hard rain, working or driving on wet soil, burning residues and loss of organic matter all break aggregates down.
Keep soil covered, return residues and compost, grow living roots most of the year, include deep-rooted and perennial plants and reduce tillage.
A meta-analysis of 89 field studies found infiltration rose on average about 59% where perennials were introduced and about 35% with cover crops, compared with conventional practice.
Compaction squeezes pores out of soil, so roots, air and water struggle to move. Bulk density is the number used to measure it.
Bulk density is dry soil weight per volume, including pores. Higher values mean fewer pores; the level that limits roots is lower for clays than for sands.

manas.q: What does a rising bulk density tell you about soil pores?

children.note: Puddles that linger, roots bending sideways or growing flat, stunted patches along wheel tracks and a spade that suddenly gets hard to push all point to compaction.

manas.q: What do roots growing sideways at one depth suggest?

children.note: Repeated ploughing or hoeing at the same depth can form a hard layer just below it. Water perches above it and roots stop there, making crops drought-prone.
Heavy machines or animals on wet soil, repeated tillage at one depth, bare soil sealing under rain and loss of organic matter.
Stay off wet soil, use fixed paths or beds, grow deep tap-rooted cover crops, add organic matter, and break a hard pan once, when the soil is dry, then keep it covered.
Push a wire flag or rod into moist soil and note where it stops, or dig a spade pit and look at roots. A core sampler and scale give an actual bulk density value.
pH measures how acid or alkaline soil is. It controls which nutrients plants can take up and how active soil life is.
pH 7 is neutral, lower is acid and higher is alkaline. Each whole unit is a ten-fold change, so pH 5 is ten times more acid than pH 6.

manas.q: How much more acid is pH 5 than pH 6?

children.note: Most crops and soil microbes do best around slightly acid to neutral. Very acid soils lock up phosphorus and lack calcium and magnesium; alkaline soils lock up iron, zinc, manganese and phosphorus.
High rainfall leaches calcium and magnesium, and years of ammonium-based fertilisers acidify soil further. Many highland maize, tea and potato fields in Kenya are strongly acid.
In strongly acid soil (roughly below pH 5–5.5), aluminium dissolves and burns root tips. Roots become short, thick and stubby, and phosphorus gets locked up even when added.

manas.q: What happens to roots when aluminium becomes toxic in acid soil?

children.note: Agricultural lime (ground calcium carbonate) raises pH and adds calcium; dolomite also adds magnesium, useful where magnesium is low. Both are generally allowed in organic farming.

manas.q: What extra nutrient does dolomite supply compared with agricultural lime?

children.note: Base the rate on a lab test (a buffer pH test), not a guess. Use finely ground lime, mix it into the topsoil some weeks before planting and re-test after a season or two.
Burnt (quick) lime and hydrated lime act fast but are harsh and are usually not permitted as soil amendments in organic certification. Gypsum does not raise pH.
Compost and manure buffer pH and bind aluminium, and wood ash or some biochars have a liming effect. They help, but on very acid soils lime is still needed.

Above about pH 7.5–8, often over limestone or in dry areas, crops show yellow young leaves from iron or zinc shortage. Add organic matter, use elemental sulphur (allowed in organic) and tolerant crops.
Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is how many positively charged nutrients a soil can hold on its surfaces and release to roots.
Clay and humus carry negative charges that hold calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium against leaching. Higher CEC means a bigger nutrient bank.

manas.q: Which two soil components give soil most of its CEC?

children.note: Smectite clays (as in black cotton soils) have high CEC; kaolinite clays of old weathered red soils have low CEC. Humus has very high CEC, so organic matter matters most in such soils.
This is the share of CEC filled by calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium rather than acidic hydrogen and aluminium. Acid soils have low base saturation.

children.topic: What it means in the field
children.note: Low-CEC sandy or red soils need smaller, more frequent feeds and lots of organic matter. High-CEC soils hold nutrients well but take more lime to shift pH.
Salt-affected soils occur mostly in dry areas and under irrigation. Saline soils have too much salt; sodic soils have too much sodium on the clay.
Excess soluble salts make it hard for roots to draw water, so crops look drought-stressed even in wet soil. White crusts appear on the surface; lab tests show high EC.

manas.q: What surface sign points to a saline soil?

children.note: Too much sodium makes clay disperse: soil seals, water stands, and dry soil sets hard. pH is often above 8.5, and dissolved organic matter can leave a dark slick crust.

manas.q: Why does sodium damage soil structure?

children.note: Patchy, stunted growth, leaf tip and edge burn, poor germination and crops wilting in moist soil. Salt-sensitive crops like beans suffer first.
Gypsum (calcium sulphate) supplies calcium that swaps places with sodium on the clay; the freed sodium is then washed below roots. Mined gypsum is allowed in organic farming.

manas.q: How does gypsum repair a sodic soil?

children.note: Apply extra good-quality water to wash salts below the root zone. It only works when the soil can drain, so fix drainage first.
Use raised beds (seed on the shoulder, away from salt build-up), mulch to cut evaporation, add organic matter and grow tolerant crops such as barley, sorghum or date palm.
India has large salt-affected (usar) areas in canal-irrigated plains; Kenya has saline and sodic patches in dry lowlands and some irrigation schemes. Test before buying gypsum.
A few major soil groups cover most farms in the region. Each has its own strengths and problems.
Deep, red, well-drained clay soils with strong blocky structure, extensive in the highlands of Kenya and Ethiopia. Very productive but often acid and low in available phosphorus.

manas.q: Which deep red soils are common in the Kenya highlands?

children.note: Dark, light and porous soils from volcanic ash, found around East African volcanoes. They hold water well but lock up phosphorus strongly.
Heavy, dark clays that swell when wet and crack deeply when dry, common in central India (regur) and parts of Kenya and Ethiopia. Fertile but sticky and prone to waterlogging.

manas.q: Why do black cotton soils crack in the dry season?

children.note: Old, deeply weathered soils rich in iron and aluminium oxides, common in southern India and parts of Africa. Low CEC, often acid and low in nutrients; organic matter is key.
Soils laid down by rivers, such as the Indo-Gangetic plain and East African river valleys. Usually fertile and easy to work; texture varies from sand to clay.
Common in arid parts of Kenya and Rajasthan. They drain fast, hold little water or nutrients, and benefit most from mulch, manure and water harvesting.
Erosion strips the richest topsoil first. Conservation slows water, keeps soil covered and holds it with roots.
Raindrops splash bare soil loose, then runoff carries it as thin sheets, small rills and finally deep gullies. Wind erosion moves dry, loose soil in open drylands.

manas.q: What are the three stages of water erosion, from smallest to largest?

children.note: Exposed roots and stones, muddy runoff, soil piled against fences, pale subsoil showing on slopes and rills after storms.
Plough, plant and build ridges across the slope along level lines, marked with a simple A-frame. Each row slows water instead of channelling it downhill.
In fanya juu, soil from a trench is thrown uphill to form a bank; over years soil collects behind it and the slope levels into terraces. Bench terraces are built level at once.

manas.q: Which way is soil thrown when digging a fanya juu terrace?

children.note: Strips of napier or vetiver grass along the contour trap soil and slow runoff, slowly forming terraces. Napier also gives fodder.

manas.q: Name a grass commonly planted in contour strips.

children.note: Keeping soil covered with crops, residues or mulch stops splash erosion at the source. Trees on bunds and agroforestry add deep roots and windbreaks.
Stop the water at the top first, then build check dams of stones or brush and plant grasses and shrubs inside the gully.
Common errors when dealing with soil properties.
Mixing small amounts of sand into clay can make it set even harder. Add organic matter instead.

manas.q: Why is adding a little sand to clay a bad idea?

children.note: Too much lime raises pH beyond the useful range and locks up micronutrients. Always test first.
Gypsum supplies calcium and sulphur and repairs sodic soils, but it does not neutralise acidity. Use lime for that.
Short videos showing these tests and practices.
Milkwood shows how to set up and read a jar test to find your soil’s texture.
UC Davis demonstrates the hand-feel ribbon method step by step.
Purdue Extension explains soil structure types and why aggregates matter.
University of Wisconsin lecture on why soils acidify and how to choose and apply lime.
FAO overview of saline and sodic soils and why they matter worldwide.
TerrAfrica shows how East African farmers build fanya juu terraces on slopes.
Authoritative references for deeper study.
FAO resources on soil classification, survey, fertility and management worldwide.
Clear guidance on soil structure, compaction and conservation practices.
East African information on soil fertility, conservation and organic farming.
Basche & DeLonge 2019: how perennials, cover crops and no-till change water entry into soil.

nodeData.note: How soil stores and supplies water, and how to use it well: field capacity and wilting point, irrigation and organic fertigation, mulching, water harvesting, drainage, water quality and drought resilience.

children.note: Soil stores rain and irrigation in its pores. How much it holds, and how much of that roots can use, depends on texture, structure and organic matter.
Large pores drain quickly after rain and refill with air; small pores hold water by capillary pull. A good soil has a mix of both.

manas.q: Which pores hold water after drainage: large or small?

children.note: Right after heavy rain or flooding, all pores are full of water and there is no air. Roots cannot breathe if this lasts more than a day or two.
The water a soil still holds after free drainage stops, usually one to three days after a soaking. It is the practical "full tank" for crops.

manas.q: What is field capacity?

children.note: The moisture level at which roots can no longer pull water and plants stay wilted even overnight. The water left is held too tightly to use.

manas.q: At what point do plants stay wilted even at night?

children.note: The water between field capacity and wilting point is what crops can use. Crops start to suffer well before it is all gone.

manas.q: Available water is the difference between which two levels?

children.note: Sands hold little available water; clays hold a lot, but much of it too tightly. Loams and silt loams usually store the most usable water.

manas.q: Which texture class usually stores the most usable water?

children.note: A crop can only use the water within reach of its roots. Breaking hard pans and encouraging deep rooting enlarges the tank.
Squeeze soil from root depth: if it forms a ball that leaves a wet mark it is near full; if it crumbles apart it is dry. Tensiometers or moisture sensors give readings.
Organic matter helps soil take in and keep water, but its biggest gains come through better structure and infiltration rather than extra storage.
Humus soaks up water like a sponge and, more importantly, glues crumbs together, creating pores that let rain soak in instead of running off.
A meta-analysis found that raising organic carbon by 1% of soil mass adds on average only about 1.2 mm of available water per 10 cm of soil, more in sands than clays.

manas.q: Does raising organic matter greatly increase available water storage?

links.label: 📄 Source: Minasny & McBratney 2018, Eur. J. Soil Sci. (meta-analysis)

children.note: Across 89 field studies, adding perennials raised infiltration by about 59% and cover crops by about 35% compared with conventional practice, so more rain enters the soil.
Keeping soil covered cuts evaporation and crusting, which often saves more water than the organic matter itself stores.
Return residues, add compost and manure, grow cover crops and reduce tillage. Benefits build up over several seasons.
The method decides how much water is wasted, how evenly it is applied and how well it suits organic inputs.
Water drips slowly from emitters onto the root zone through pipes. It wastes little water and keeps leaves dry, but needs clean water and good filters.

manas.q: Why does drip irrigation reduce leaf diseases?

children.note: Sprays water over the crop like rain. Suits uneven land and lighter soils but loses water to wind and evaporation and wets leaves, which can favour disease.
Water flows along furrows or floods level basins. Cheap and simple, but uses more water and can waterlog low spots or bring up salts if poorly managed.
Consider water supply and quality, soil type, slope, crop value, labour and budget. Low-cost gravity drip kits suit small plots of vegetables.
Irrigate before stress, typically when around half of the available water in the root zone has been used. FAO Paper 56 gives depletion fractions by crop.

manas.q: Roughly what share of available water is commonly allowed to deplete before irrigating?

children.note: Too much water leaches nutrients, starves roots of air, raises water tables and salts, and invites root rots.
Fertigation feeds crops through the irrigation system. Organic and biological liquids can be used, but solids and slime must be kept out of pipes and emitters.
Feeding dissolved nutrients or microbial products into irrigation water so they reach the root zone in small, frequent doses.
Clogging comes from fine particles, chemical deposits (such as lime scale or iron) and slimy biofilms of bacteria. Organic liquids add all three risks.

manas.q: What are the three main causes of drip emitter clogging?

children.note: A study of drip lines carrying biogas slurry found clogging grew over time and was worst at the far end of laterals; deposits were sticky mixes of fine particles and microbial slime.

links.label: 📄 Source: Wang et al. 2022, Sci. Total Environ.

children.note: Let manure teas or slurry settle, decant the clear liquid, strain through fine cloth and dilute well before injecting. Never inject thick or fibrous liquids.

Use a screen or disc filter sized for your emitters, plus a settling tank or sand filter for dirty water. Inject upstream of the main filter so it catches particles from the inputs, and clean filters often during fertigation.

manas.q: Where should the filter sit relative to the fertiliser injection point?

children.note: Inject biological products in the middle of an irrigation run so the system is already full, then run clean water to flush lines. Avoid chlorinated water and copper at the same time.
Open lateral ends regularly to flush sediment. For cleaning, use only agents your organic standard permits; check with your certifier before using acids or chlorine.
Venturi injectors, small dosing pumps or a header tank on gravity drip can all feed liquids. Always inject upstream of the main filter.
A mulch is a cover laid on the soil surface. It keeps moisture in, keeps soil cool and stops crusting and erosion.
Mulch cuts evaporation, protects soil from raindrop impact, smothers weeds, moderates temperature and, if organic, feeds soil life as it rots.

manas.q: Name three ways mulch saves soil water or protects soil.

children.note: Straw, maize stover, dry grass, leaves, coffee husks and tree prunings. Use what is available locally and keep it a few centimetres clear of stems.
Low-growing cover crops such as dolichos lablab or mucuna cover the soil while growing and add nitrogen if they are legumes.
A meta-analysis of 74 studies on maize and wheat found mulching raised yields and water-use efficiency, by up to 60%, with bigger gains for maize and in drier conditions.

manas.q: Did mulching help more in wet or dry conditions?

links.label: 📄 Source: Qin et al. 2015, Scientific Reports (meta-analysis)

children.note: Plastic raises yields in dry areas, but leftover fragments build up and harm yields at high levels. Organic standards generally allow it only if fully removed after use.

links.label: 📄 Source: Gao et al. 2019, Sci. Total Environ. (meta-analysis)

children.note: Mulch piled against stems invites rots and pests; sawdust mixed into soil can tie up nitrogen; termites may eat dry mulch in drylands, so add manure or use tougher material.
Catching and storing rain where it falls, or collecting runoff, so crops get more water in dry spells.
Small pits roughly 15–50 cm across and 5–15 cm deep, filled with manure or compost and planted. They catch runoff and concentrate nutrients right at the roots.

manas.q: What goes into a zaï pit besides the seed?

children.note: Traditional in the western Sahel and revived in Burkina Faso by farmer Yacouba Sawadogo, zaï pits are now also used in dry counties of Kenya such as Kitui.
Semicircular earth bunds dug on gentle slopes with the open side facing uphill, catching runoff for trees, sorghum or pasture inside the curve.

manas.q: Which way does the open side of a half-moon face?

children.note: Ridges and furrows with small cross-ties every few metres, making boxes that hold rain where it falls instead of letting it run down the furrow.

manas.q: What do the cross-ties in tied ridges do?

children.note: Dug ponds collect runoff for supplementary irrigation and livestock. Use a silt trap at the inlet, line with clay or a dam liner and shade or cover to cut evaporation.
Gutters into tanks supply kitchen gardens and nurseries; road and path runoff can be guided into pits or fields with small channels.
Too much water is as harmful as too little: roots need air. Good drainage keeps soil breathing.
Yellowing and wilting despite wet soil, stunted growth, grey or blue-green subsoil with rusty mottles, sour or rotten-egg smell and water standing after rain.

manas.q: What subsoil colours suggest frequent waterlogging?

children.note: Without oxygen roots die back, nitrogen is lost as gas by denitrification, and root rot organisms such as Pythium and Phytophthora thrive.

manas.q: How is nitrogen lost from waterlogged soil?

children.note: Shape land so water runs off gently, use raised or cambered beds and open ditches to carry excess water away.
On vertisols, broad raised beds separated by furrows (developed by ICRISAT in India) drain excess water while the beds hold moisture for the crop.
Break hard pans when dry, grow deep-rooted plants and add organic matter so water can move down. Subsurface drains suit high-value land.
Not all water is good for irrigation. Test sources, especially boreholes in dry areas, before investing in a system.
Electrical conductivity shows total dissolved salt. Higher EC water adds salt with every irrigation, so it needs salt-tolerant crops and extra water to leach.

manas.q: What does the EC of irrigation water measure?

links.label: 📄 Source: FAO Water Quality for Agriculture (Paper 29)

children.note: The sodium adsorption ratio compares sodium with calcium and magnesium. High-SAR water slowly makes soil sodic, sealing the surface.

manas.q: What problem does high-SAR water cause in soil?

children.note: Boron, chloride and bicarbonate can harm sensitive crops even when total salt is moderate. Bicarbonate also leaves white scale on drippers and leaves.

links.label: 📄 Source: FAO Water Quality for Agriculture (Paper 29)

children.note: Water with dissolved iron turns rusty in pipes and feeds iron bacteria that clog emitters. Aerate and settle it before filtering.
Water polluted by sewage or manure can carry E. coli and other pathogens onto crops eaten raw. Organic and food-safety rules require clean water for such crops.
Send a sample to a soil and water lab for EC, pH, SAR, major ions and, for food crops, a microbial test. Retest boreholes yearly or after floods.
Combining soil, crop and water practices lets farms carry on through dry spells.
Covered, high-organic-matter soils take in more rain and lose less to runoff and evaporation, buying crops extra days in a dry spell.
Breaking pans, avoiding over-watering early and encouraging deep roots lets crops reach stored subsoil water.
Mycorrhizal fungi extend fine threads beyond the root zone and can help plants take up water and phosphorus in dry soil.

manas.q: How do mycorrhizal fungi help plants in dry soil?

children.note: Sorghum, millets, cowpea, pigeon pea and cassava handle drought better than maize; early-maturing varieties escape late-season dry spells.
Flowering and grain fill are most sensitive to water stress, so save harvested or limited irrigation water for these stages.
Hedges, windbreaks and scattered trees slow drying winds and shade soil, reducing evaporation from fields.
Short videos on soil water and water-saving practices.
An animated explanation of how soil holds water between field capacity and wilting point.

The Australian Wine Research Institute on checking filters, flushing lines and keeping emitters clear.

children.note: Smart Water for Agriculture (Kenya) guide to building a farm water pan.
Authoritative references for deeper study.

nodeData.note: How to tell whether a soil is healthy, from simple spade and water tests in the field to laboratory analysis. Includes how to sample correctly and read a soil report.

children.note: A healthy soil works as a living system: it takes in water, feeds crops, supports diverse life and resists erosion. A degraded soil has lost structure, organic matter and life.
Dark, crumbly topsoil, plenty of earthworms, deep roots, quick water entry, an earthy smell and residues that break down within a season.
Even crop growth, deep roots with fine root hairs and fewer stress symptoms in dry spells point to good soil. Legume roots with pink nodules show active nitrogen fixation.

manas.q: What colour are active nitrogen-fixing nodules inside?

children.note: Crusting after rain, puddles and run-off, hard plough pans, pale colour, few worms, sour smell and residues that stay undecomposed.

Yellowing of older leaves suggests nitrogen shortage; purple tinge can mean phosphorus shortage; scorched leaf edges can mean potassium shortage; stripes on young leaves often mean zinc or iron problems. Confirm with tests before acting.
White crusts on the surface point to salts, while black slick crusts and very slow drainage suggest sodicity. These are common in irrigated drylands of India and parts of Kenya.
Soil health is assessed through physical (structure, water entry), chemical (pH, nutrients, salts) and biological (organic matter, life, respiration) indicators. Good assessment combines all three.

manas.q: What are the three groups of soil health indicators?

children.note: Many soil health checks need only a spade, a can, water and a notebook. Repeat them in the same place and season each year to see trends.
Dig a block of soil about a spade deep and examine it. Look at structure, colour, roots, smell, worms and any hard layers.
Good soil crumbles into rounded aggregates, roots grow straight down and there are worm channels. Flat plates, sideways-turning roots or a sudden hard layer signal compaction.

manas.q: What does a root that turns sideways in a spade test usually indicate?

children.note: Dig in a field and in an undisturbed spot such as a fence line or forest edge. The difference shows how much management has changed the soil.
Gently place dry soil clods in water and watch. Stable, biologically active soil stays together, while weak soil quickly falls apart and clouds the water.
Aggregates held together by roots, fungal hyphae, glomalin and microbial glues resist breaking apart in water. Tilled, low-organic-matter soil lacks these binders.

manas.q: In a slake test, what does a clod that falls apart quickly tell you?

children.note: Push a metal ring or open-ended can into the soil, pour in a fixed volume of water and time how long it takes to soak in. Slow infiltration means more run-off and erosion.
Insert the ring a few centimetres deep, line it with plastic, add the water, then pull away the plastic and start timing. Do a second run as the soil is then near field moisture.
Compare times between fields, between tilled and untilled patches, or over years. A falling time over seasons shows improving structure.
Dig a spade-sized block of topsoil when soil is moist and count earthworms. Seasonal timing matters, as worms move deep in dry or hot periods.
Ten or more worms in a spadeful is a commonly used sign of good biological health. Very few or none suggests low organic matter, disturbance or chemical harm.

manas.q: Roughly how many earthworms per spadeful is commonly taken as a good sign?

children.note: Healthy soil smells sweet and earthy because of geosmin from actinomycetes. A sour or rotten-egg smell suggests waterlogging and lack of oxygen.
Dark topsoil usually means more organic matter. Grey or blue-grey patches and mottles show poor drainage, while pale topsoil suggests low organic matter or erosion.

manas.q: What do grey or blue-grey mottles in soil indicate?

children.note: Bury a piece of cotton cloth or check last season's residues. Fast breakdown shows active microbes; residues that remain intact suggest weak biology.
Shake soil with water in a jar and let it settle; sand settles in a minute, silt in hours and clay over a day. The layers give a rough idea of soil texture.
A soil lab measures what cannot be seen in the field. Basic tests guide fertiliser and lime use; biological tests show how alive the soil is.
pH measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, on a scale of 0–14. Most crops grow best around pH 6.0–7.5.
pH controls nutrient availability: phosphorus is locked up in very acid and very alkaline soils, and aluminium becomes toxic below about pH 5.5. Many beneficial bacteria prefer near-neutral soil.

manas.q: What pH range suits most crops?

children.note: Acid soils (common in high-rainfall Kenya highlands and NE India) are corrected with agricultural lime. Alkaline and sodic soils may need gypsum and organic matter.
Electrical conductivity measures dissolved salts in soil. On Soil Health Cards, EC below 1 dS/m is normal; higher values can harm germination and sensitive crops.

manas.q: What does soil EC measure?

links.label: 📄 Source: Soil Health Card, Govt of India

children.note: Organic carbon is the main lab indicator of organic matter. Indian Soil Health Card ratings treat below 0.5% as low, 0.5–0.75% as medium and above 0.75% as high.

manas.q: On India's Soil Health Card, what organic carbon level is rated low?

links.label: 📄 Source: Soil Health Card, Govt of India

children.note: Labs report available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, usually in kg/ha in India and mg/kg (ppm) in many other labs.
Commonly used ratings: available N low below 280, medium 280–560, high above 560 kg/ha; P (Olsen) low below 10, medium 10–25, high above 25; K low below 110, medium 110–280, high above 280 kg/ha.

links.label: 📄 Source: Soil Health Card, Govt of India

children.note: Phosphorus values depend on the extraction method, such as Olsen for neutral-alkaline soils or Bray/Mehlich for acid soils. Compare results only within the same method.
Labs can test sulphur, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, manganese, copper and boron. Zinc deficiency is widespread in Indian and Kenyan soils.
Commonly used critical limits by DTPA extraction are about 0.6 ppm zinc, 4.5 ppm iron and 0.2 ppm copper, and about 0.5 ppm hot-water-soluble boron. Below these, crops may respond to application.
Cation exchange capacity is the soil's ability to hold positively charged nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium. Clay and organic matter raise CEC; sandy soils have low CEC.

manas.q: What does cation exchange capacity (CEC) tell you?

children.note: Texture (sand, silt, clay) shapes drainage and nutrient holding. Bulk density shows compaction; higher values mean fewer pores for air and roots.
Microbial biomass carbon measures the amount of living microbes in soil. It responds faster than total organic carbon to changes in management.
Respiration tests measure the burst of CO2 released when dried soil is re-wetted, showing how active microbes are. The Solvita CO2-burst test is one widely used method.
Higher CO2 release generally means more active biology and more nutrients being released from organic matter. Compare soils tested by the same lab and method.

manas.q: What does a soil respiration (CO2-burst) test measure?

children.note: Some labs offer active carbon (permanganate oxidisable carbon), enzyme activity, potentially mineralisable nitrogen and phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) profiles. These are useful for tracking change over time.
A test is only as good as the sample. A sample must represent the field, so it is made by mixing many small cores.
Sample after harvest and before the next crop, at least two to three months after fertiliser or manure application. Sample the same field at the same time of year for comparisons.
Treat each field or uniform area separately and walk in a zig-zag pattern, taking 10–20 spots. Avoid bunds, field edges, manure heaps, trees, compost pits and waterlogged spots.

manas.q: How many spots are usually combined into one composite sample?

children.note: For field crops, take soil from the top 0–15 cm (plough layer). For orchards and deep-rooted crops, sample deeper layers such as 0–30 and 30–60 cm separately.

manas.q: What depth is sampled for most field crops?

children.note: Clear surface litter, dig a V-shaped pit to the sampling depth and slice a thin, even layer of soil from one side. This gives equal soil from every depth.
Mix all cores in a clean bucket or on a sheet, then divide into four, discard two opposite quarters and repeat until about half a kilo remains.
Dry the sample in shade, never in an oven or direct sun, and pack it in a clean cloth or plastic bag. Label with farmer name, field, crop history, depth and date.
For microbial tests, keep samples cool and send them quickly as advised by the lab, because microbes change in a hot bag. Do not mix with fertiliser bags or chemicals.
A soil report lists measured values with ratings and often fertiliser recommendations. Read it as a whole, not one number at a time.
If pH or salts are far from normal, fix them first, because they control how much any nutrient can be used.
Low organic carbon means low biological activity and poor nutrient holding. Plan compost, manure, cover crops and residue retention alongside fertiliser.
Use the ratings (low, medium, high) with the crop's needs to adjust doses. Medium or high ratings may allow reduced application.
Yield is limited by the nutrient in shortest supply, so a zinc or sulphur gap can waste added NPK. Fix the most limiting factor first.

manas.q: Why can a micronutrient deficiency waste NPK fertiliser?

children.note: One test is a snapshot; tests every two to three years from the same field show whether management is improving the soil.
Poor sampling, comparing results from different lab methods and acting on one number are the most common errors. Units such as ppm, mg/kg and kg/ha must not be mixed up.
Both countries have public and private soil testing networks. Farmers can often get tests at low cost through government programmes.
The Soil Health Card scheme gives farmers a card with test results and crop-wise fertiliser advice for their land. Samples are tested in state and district soil testing labs.

manas.q: What does India's Soil Health Card give farmers?

links.label: 📄 Source: Soil Health Card, Govt of India

children.note: Krishi Vigyan Kendras, state agriculture departments and agricultural universities run soil testing labs and help farmers take samples. Some offer mobile testing vans.
The Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization runs soil and plant analysis services and research on soil fertility. County extension officers can advise on sampling.
Accredited private labs in Nairobi and other towns offer soil, plant tissue and water tests. Rapid in-field kits and scanners are spreading but should be checked against a lab.
Choose a lab that uses standard methods, explains its units and gives crop-specific advice. Use the same lab over time for comparable results.
Short videos on this topic from universities, extension services and experienced growers. Opens YouTube.

nodeData.note: How soils store carbon, which farm practices build it, how much evidence backs them, and the limits. Also covers soil nitrous oxide and methane, measuring carbon, carbon credits and drought resilience.

children.note: Soil holds more organic carbon than all plants on land. Small changes in this huge store matter for both the climate and farm fertility.
Soil is the largest land reservoir of organic carbon, larger than all vegetation. Losing even a few percent releases a lot of CO₂.

manas.q: Which holds more organic carbon on land: soils or vegetation?

links.label: 📄 Source: Georgiou et al. 2022, Nature Communications

children.note: Soil carbon rises only when carbon going in (roots, residues, manure) is greater than carbon lost as CO₂ when microbes decompose it, or by erosion.
Organic carbon comes from living things; inorganic carbon is mostly carbonate (lime) in dry and alkaline soils. Farm practices mainly change the organic part.
Soil organic matter (SOM) is all the organic material; soil organic carbon (SOC) is the carbon in it, roughly half of SOM by weight. Lab reports may give either.
Mineral-bound carbon in topsoil is only about 42% of what the minerals could hold, and farmed soils are among the most under-filled. Under-filled soils gain carbon fastest.

manas.q: Do soils far below their carbon capacity gain carbon faster or slower?

links.label: 📄 Source: Georgiou et al. 2022, Nature Communications

children.note: Plants capture CO₂ by photosynthesis; roots and microbes then move part of that carbon into forms that can stay in soil for years to centuries.
Carbon from roots stays in soil much longer than carbon from leaves and stems. Root carbon is a main source of stable soil organic matter.

manas.q: Which contributes more to lasting soil carbon: roots or above-ground residues?

links.label: 📄 Source: Rasse et al. 2005, Plant and Soil

children.note: Living roots leak sugars, acids and other compounds. Microbes eat them quickly and turn part of them into their own bodies, which later become soil carbon.
Carbon entering below ground, through roots and exudates, forms stable soil carbon more efficiently than surface litter.
Dead microbial cells and their residues (necromass) can make up more than half of soil organic carbon in farm, grassland and forest topsoils.

manas.q: What is microbial necromass, and how much of soil carbon can it be?

links.label: 📄 Source: Liang et al. 2019, Global Change Biology

children.note: Easily digested plant inputs are used efficiently by microbes, and their products bond to soil minerals. So 'labile' food can still build stable carbon.

links.label: 📄 Source: Cotrufo et al. 2013, Global Change Biology

children.note: Fungal hyphae, roots and microbial glues bind soil into crumbs (aggregates). Carbon inside is hidden from decomposers; tillage breaks them open.
Scientists now split soil organic matter into two pools with very different behaviour. Knowing which one a practice builds tells you how long the gain lasts.
Partly decomposed plant fragments. It builds up quickly, feeds soil life and nutrient supply, but is easily lost again when management changes.

manas.q: What is POM and how stable is it?

links.label: 📄 Source: Lavallee et al. 2020, Global Change Biology

children.note: Small, mostly microbial molecules bonded to clay and silt. It persists for decades to centuries but fills up (saturates) as mineral surfaces are used.

manas.q: Why is MAOM more stable than POM?

links.label: 📄 Source: Lavallee et al. 2020, Global Change Biology

children.note: Mineral-associated carbon is about 66% of carbon in surface soils and 70% in deeper layers, roughly 899 billion tonnes to 1 m depth worldwide.

links.label: 📄 Source: Georgiou et al. 2022, Nature Communications

children.note: Clay and silt soils can store more MAOM than sandy soils. On sands, carbon gains are mostly POM and need continuous inputs to keep.
Practices work by adding more carbon (roots, residues, manure) or losing less (less disturbance, cover). Meta-analyses show real but modest and site-dependent gains.
A meta-analysis of 37 sites found cover crops added about 0.32 t C/ha/yr; modelled gains level off after many decades at about 17 t C/ha in the top 22 cm.

manas.q: About how much carbon per year do cover crops add, according to Poeplau & Don?

links.label: 📄 Source: Poeplau & Don 2015, Agric. Ecosyst. Environ.

children.note: Returning straw raised SOC concentration by about 13% on average across 176 studies, with gains slowing after about 12 years. In paddies it also raised methane.

manas.q: What is the main climate trade-off of returning straw to rice paddies?

links.label: 📄 Source: Liu et al. 2014, Global Change Biology

children.note: Manure raised SOC stocks by about 35% (about 10.7 t C/ha) on average across 101 studies, most in low-carbon soils. Note: much of that carbon was moved from elsewhere, not newly removed from air.

manas.q: Why does manure-built soil carbon not always count as new climate removal?

children.note: In UK trials over 150+ years, heavy yearly farmyard manure gave large SOC rises for 40–60 years before slowing. Most ordinary treatments gained less.

links.label: 📄 Source: Poulton et al. 2018, Global Change Biology

children.note: Adding trees to cropland or pasture stores carbon in wood and usually raises soil carbon too, especially when cropland is converted.

links.label: 📄 Source: De Stefano & Jacobson 2018, Agroforestry Systems

children.note: Charcoal made for soil. A review of 26 meta-analyses found overall benefits for yield, soil properties and soil carbon; poor-quality biochars cause most bad results.

manas.q: What did a review of 26 meta-analyses conclude about biochar?

links.label: 📄 Source: Schmidt et al. 2021, GCB Bioenergy

children.note: Works best on acidic, coarse, tropical soils; very high rates can harm. It is costly, and feedstock must be clean residue, not trees cut for the purpose.
Grazing can raise or lower soil carbon depending on rainfall, soil texture, grass type and grazing pressure. There is no single right answer.

manas.q: Does grazing always increase grassland soil carbon?

links.label: 📄 Source: McSherry & Ritchie 2013, Global Change Biology

children.note: No-till often moves carbon to the surface rather than adding more; deep sampling frequently shows small net gains. It still reduces erosion.

links.label: 📄 Source: Powlson et al. 2014, Nature Climate Change

children.note: Legumes, deep-rooted perennials and longer rotations keep living roots in soil for more months, adding below-ground carbon.
Soil carbon is valuable for farming, but its climate role is often oversold. Know the limits before making promises.
Soils fill up: gains slow and stop at a new balance. Including saturation cuts estimated climate benefits of soil carbon sequestration by 53–81% to 2100.

manas.q: What is soil carbon saturation and how much does it reduce climate estimates?

links.label: 📄 Source: Moinet et al. 2023, Global Change Biology

children.note: Carbon built over years can be lost quickly by ploughing, drought, fire or land sale. Gains are reversible unless practices continue.

manas.q: Why is permanence a problem for soil carbon?

children.note: Even the most promising soil methods together are unlikely to offset more than about 5% of yearly fossil-fuel CO₂.

links.label: 📄 Source: Schlesinger & Amundson 2019, Global Change Biology

children.note: Across 21+ meta-analyses, yield responses to more soil carbon ranged from negative to positive. 'Win-win' holds only under specific conditions.

links.label: 📄 Source: Moinet et al. 2023, Global Change Biology

children.topic: Carbon for soils, not soils for carbon
children.note: Build organic matter mainly for fertility, water and resilience; treat any climate benefit as a bonus.

links.label: 📄 Source: Moinet et al. 2023, Global Change Biology

children.note: Soils also emit two strong greenhouse gases. Practices that add carbon can raise these gases, so the whole balance must be counted.
Nitrous oxide is about 270–300 times stronger than CO₂ over 100 years and also damages the ozone layer. Fertilised soils are its main human source.

manas.q: Why does nitrous oxide matter so much for farming's climate impact?

children.note: Global N₂O emissions are about 17 Tg N per year; human-caused emissions, mostly from cropland nitrogen, rose 30% in four decades to about 7.3 Tg N.
Microbes release N₂O during nitrification and especially denitrification, which peaks when soils are wet, warm and rich in nitrate and fresh carbon.
Match nitrogen to crop need, split doses, use legumes, avoid waterlogging and do not pile large amounts of manure or urine on wet soils.
Flooded paddies lack oxygen, so methane-producing archaea thrive. Fresh straw or green manure in flooded soil increases methane.

manas.q: Why do flooded rice fields release methane?

children.note: Letting paddies dry periodically cut methane by about 52% versus continuous flooding, but raised N₂O by about 44%; net warming fell about 47%.

manas.q: What does alternate wetting and drying do to methane and N₂O?

children.note: Well-drained, undisturbed soils host bacteria that consume methane. Compaction and heavy nitrogen use weaken this sink.
MRV means measurement, reporting and verification. It is the hardest and most expensive part of soil carbon projects.
Yearly changes are tiny compared with the total stock and vary a lot across a field, so many samples over several years are needed to detect change.

manas.q: Why is soil carbon change hard to measure?

links.label: 📄 Source: Smith et al. 2020, Global Change Biology

children.note: Carbon stock = % carbon × bulk density × depth. Without bulk density (and equivalent soil mass), changes in compaction can fake gains or losses.

manas.q: Which measurement besides %C is needed to calculate a soil carbon stock?

children.note: Sampling only the top 15–20 cm can mistake carbon moved by tillage for new carbon. At least 30 cm, and deeper where possible, is preferred.
Dry combustion (elemental analyser) is the reference. Older wet-oxidation (Walkley–Black) is cheaper but less complete; do not mix methods over time.

children.topic: New tools: spectroscopy, models, remote sensing
children.note: Infrared spectroscopy, process models, benchmark sites and satellites can cut costs, but must be calibrated with real soil samples.

links.label: 📄 Source: Smith et al. 2020, Global Change Biology

children.note: Companies pay for verified carbon removal. For farmers it can be extra income, but contracts, costs and science bring real risks.
A project registers fields, changes practices, measures or models carbon gain, gets it verified to a standard, and sells credits; farmers receive a share.
Credits are valid only if the change would not have happened anyway, the carbon stays, and emissions are not just pushed elsewhere.

manas.q: What do additionality, permanence and leakage mean in carbon credits?

links.label: 📄 Source: Paul et al. 2023, J. Environ. Management

children.note: A 2023 review concluded private soil carbon certificates are unlikely to deliver the offsets claimed, mainly because permanence cannot be guaranteed.

links.label: 📄 Source: Paul et al. 2023, J. Environ. Management

children.note: Different crediting methods for the same practice in nearby regions undermine credibility; scientists call for regionally consistent rules.
For conservation agriculture in Bihar and Punjab, potential credit earnings were only about US$18–30 per hectare; residue-burning bans also affect eligibility.

manas.q: Roughly how much could Indian farmers earn per hectare from conservation-agriculture carbon credits?

children.note: Smallholder projects need aggregation of thousands of farms; measurement and middlemen costs eat much of the price. Adoption depends on land, literacy and support.
Before signing: contract length, who owns the credits and data, payment share and timing, penalties if carbon is lost, and whether the land can be sold.
The surest benefits of more organic matter are for the farm itself: better structure, water entry and steadier yields in bad seasons.
Across 60 studies, 1% more organic carbon raised available water by only about 1.2 mm per 100 mm of soil on average; more in sands, least in clays.

manas.q: How much does 1% more soil organic carbon increase available water capacity?

links.label: 📄 Source: Minasny & McBratney 2018, Eur. J. Soil Sci.

children.note: Better aggregates, roots and earthworm channels let rain soak in instead of running off, which often matters more in drought than water storage itself.
Residue cover lowers soil temperature and evaporation and protects against raindrop crusting and erosion.
Maize and wheat yields rise with soil carbon up to about 2% SOC, then level off; about two-thirds of such land is below 2%.

manas.q: At about what soil organic carbon level do maize and wheat yield gains level off?

children.note: Hot climates decompose organic matter fast, so inputs must be steady. In Kenya manure is scarce; in India stopping residue burning is a quick win for soil and air.
